papers.title: Spherical Physics-informed Neural Operator with Multi-scale Coupling for Meteorological Downscaling
papers.abstract: Meteorological downscaling is crucial for high-resolution regional climate forecasting and disaster early warning. While neural operators have emerged as a promising paradigm for modeling complex spatiotemporal mappings, existing frameworks often struggle with spherical manifold geometric distortions, inherent atmospheric multi-scale coupling mismatches, and lack of explicit atmospheric laws. We propose the Spherical Physics-informed Neural Operator, which utilizes a Spherical Laplacian Decomposition to partition atmospheric fields into hierarchical frequency components, maintaining exact point-wise correspondence across scales. To evaluate these representations at arbitrary locations, we introduce a localized spherical integral operator that approximates continuous kernel transforms via geometry-aware attention. Dynamical consistency is further enforced by embedding differentiable constraints into the learning process. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework attains superior accuracy and zero-shot generalization across various meteorological variables and unseen queries, representing a robust and interpretable solution for global-to-regional meteorological downscaling.

papers.title: AirMPA: A Meteorology-to-Pollution Adapter for Global Air Quality Forecasting
papers.abstract: Accurate real-time forecasting of atmospheric pollutants is essential for reducing exposure risks and improving public health. Traditional numerical forecasting systems suffer from incomplete parameterizations, uncertain inputs, and high computational cost. Existing deep learning approaches improve efficiency, but often entangle meteorological and pollutant variables within unified forecasting frameworks, limiting flexibility and pollutant-specific representation learning. To address these challenges, we propose AirMPA, a decoupled autoregressive framework for meteorology-to-pollution forecasting. AirMPA predicts 13 atmospheric pollutants at 0.4{\deg} spatial resolution and 12-h temporal resolution using meteorological fields, emission priors, and historical pollutant concentrations. The model is built on an improved Swin-Transformer architecture with zonal release attention and dual-branch fusion, enabling more effective modeling of global transport continuity and heterogeneous pollutant dynamics. During training, AirMPA uses the fifth-generation atmospheric reanalysis from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ERA5) as meteorological forcing, while during inference it directly ingests forecast fields from external meteorological models, enabling stable autoregressive prediction up to 5 days ahead. Experiments show that AirMPA consistently outperforms Aurora and surpasses the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) in approximately 90% of pollutant-lead-time evaluation cases over the 5-day forecast horizon, while outperforming CAMS on all variables beyond 48 h. These results demonstrate the potential of decoupled meteorology-to-pollution forecasting for global air quality prediction.

papers.title: BridgeCast: Bridging Ocean Wave Forecasts to Reanalysis via Flow Matching with Exogenous Variables
papers.abstract: Ocean wave forecasting is essential for maritime safety, offshore operations, and coastal resilience, yet remains challenging due to systematic biases in physics-based models. Physical models, while widely used, rely on approximations and parameterizations that limit their accuracy under complex ocean-atmosphere conditions. To enhance ocean wave forecasting, we propose BridgeCast, within a physics-AI hybrid framework for bias correction. BridgeCast is a probabilistic model based on conditional flow matching (CFM) that learns to transform physical model forecasts into reanalysis-like fields. It treats physical forecasts as corrupted observations and employs a continuous-time generative process to bridge their distribution toward that of reanalysis data. BridgeCast is parameterized by a Transformer-based architecture that enables spatiotemporal modeling, incorporation of exogenous atmospheric variables, and flexible inference via both ordinary and stochastic differential equation formulations. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that BridgeCast consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across regions and forecast lead times.

papers.title: Wet-Biased Data Pipelines Mislead the Training and Evaluation of Generative Precipitation Nowcasting
papers.abstract: Generative models for precipitation nowcasting are trained and evaluated predominantly on wet-biased datasets, which over-represent precipitation events to emphasize rare extremes. Selecting test cases based on target observations is known to favor forecasts that match the selected distribution rather than the intended deployment distribution. We show analytically how this target-dependent sampling also shifts the conditional distribution learned by generative models. When training and test sampling match, even an ideal model learns precisely the distribution favored by evaluation, allowing the evaluation bias to conceal the training bias. Using a fixed satellite-to-radar diffusion model, we demonstrate that target-dependent test sampling can reverse the calibration assessment. The model appears under-predictive on a wet-biased test set but over-predictive on a deployment-representative test set. This result is replicated outside the model's training domain after a seven-year gap. Utilizing classifier-free guidance as an example, we demonstrate how the contradictory calibration assessment can misdirect downstream model development.

papers.title: Interpretability of AI weather models via intermediate decoding
papers.abstract: AI weather prediction models are often regarded as black boxes. Despite their impressive skill, there is little understanding of how the input data is processed during inference to produce the forecast. This limitation arises from the use of high-dimensional latent representations in which individual dimensions are no longer directly interpretable in physical terms. To gain insight into how forecasts are constructed, we propose the method of intermediate decoding for AI weather models and apply it to GraphCast, Aurora and ArchesWeather. In this approach, latent states from intermediate depths are decoded back into meteorological fields. To do this, we use the decoder that has been trained to output the forecast at the end of processing. Since latent states at different depths do not share a consistent basis, we train affine transformations that align intermediate latent states with the decoder's expected input space. Applying this framework to the three models yields the following results. First, the skill of forecasts at intermediate stages of processing improves gradually through the processor layers. Second, bypassing all processor blocks shows that the encoder-decoder pair is not an identity mapping returning the input, but instead plays a significant role in the forecast construction. Third, by examining increments of individual processor blocks across model depth, we show that all three models progressively refine the forecast from coarse to finer spatial scales. Finally, we assess the physical consistency of the intermediate decoding forecasts and find that large scales remain physically balanced throughout processing, while small scales become more balanced with each additional processor block.

papers.title: UDL-RT: A unified differentiable all-sky microwave radiative transfer model with learnable parameterizations
papers.abstract: Radiance-based retrievals and data assimilation require radiative transfer models (RTMs) to simulate radiances and quantify their sensitivities to atmospheric and surface conditions. Conventional RTMs often rely on separately maintained forward, tangent-linear, and adjoint codes, complicating model development and extension. Here, we present the Unified Differentiable and Learnable Radiative Transfer model (UDL-RT), a PyTorch-based framework for all-sky microwave radiative transfer that couples neural-network (NN) parameterizations of gaseous absorption, hydrometeor bulk scattering properties (BSPs), and ocean surface emissivity with an explicit radiative transfer solver in a unified differentiable computational graph. Automatic differentiation directly computes Jacobians with respect to input variables, reducing the model maintenance burden. The NN parameterizations offer flexible representations of complex nonlinear relationships. For example, the NN gas-absorption parameterization reduces the standard deviation of brightness-temperature (TB) errors by approximately 60-85% in the water-vapour channels compared with linear regression. Moreover, UDL-RT propagates loss gradients to trainable parameters to optimize physical parameterizations against observations, with GPU-accelerated batched computation supporting efficient iterative learning. Using Microwave Humidity Sounder-2 (MWHS-2) observations, we optimize the snow BSP parameterization through gradient-based learning. The optimized parameterization improves agreement between simulated and observed TB distributions and reduces the systematic bias and skewness of observation-minus-background (O-B) departures. Overall, UDL-RT integrates radiance simulation, sensitivity analysis, and parameterization optimization within a unified framework, supporting future remote sensing retrieval and data assimilation applications.

papers.title: Spatio-temporal precipitation downscaling at hourly resolution based on km-scale regional simulations
papers.abstract: Effectively preparing for changes in extreme flooding requires understanding present and future rainfall extremes with return periods up to $\sim$100-1000 years, including changes in intensity, spatial structure at km-scale and sub-daily temporal variability. Conventional km-scale climate models give greatly increased realism compared to typical global climate models (GCMs) but are too computationally costly to allow enough simulations for robustly quantifying changes in extremes. This work presents an approach based on video diffusion to generate realistic precipitation at 8.8km-hourly resolution by spatially and temporally downscaling daily, GCM-scale atmospheric variables. The emulator is trained to produce similar output to a $4\times$-coarsening of the Met Office's 2.2km-resolution UK convection-permitting model. An application for such an emulator is to downscale large-ensemble GCM simulations to allow quantification of $\sim$100-1000-year return level rainfall, which in turn can be used to drive hydrological and flood models for improved projections of future changes in flood risk.

papers.title: Transient growth and Counter-propagating Rossby Waves in a sloped Eady problem
papers.abstract: A mechanistic interpretation for baroclinic normal mode instability with exponential growth is the interaction arising from Counter-propagating Rossby Waves (CRWs), where pairs of CRWs phase-lock and interfere constructively. On the other hand, an arbitrary initial condition can lead to finite transient growth as long as there is constructive interference. The present work investigates the characteristics of finite time transient instabilities and its description in terms of CRWs in a baroclinic system with asymmetric interaction, in contrast to usual settings where there is an inherent symmetry that leads to equal and opposite CRWs. A sloped Eady problem on a $f$-plane is considered here, which has the benefit that there are only two CRWs in the system, and the presence of a bottom topographic slope can be formulated in a such a way that only one of the CRW is affected and controlled by a single parameter representing the asymmetry, via modifying the bottom background potential vorticity gradient. We derive conditions where the instantaneous growths have key CRW properties that are independent of the asymmetry parameter for a reasonably general family of norms, and that the instability characteristic in the total energy norm is entirely independent of the asymmetry parameter. For finite time transient growth, the optimal initial condition is in some sense counter to that of the exponential growing normal mode: where the bottom slope is such that it is strengthening the bottom CRW, the normal mode has a larger bottom CRW, but the finite time optimal initial condition wants the bottom CRW to be weak instead, and vice-versa. While the results presented here are for the sloped Eady problem, the same results were also found for an analogous Phillips problem, and we speculate the instability characteristics may have origins in the underlying symmetries that are common to those two problems.

papers.title: Coarse-grained local available potential energy
papers.abstract: The available potential energy (APE) of a fluid can be defined locally in space, providing useful insights into both the energetics and dynamics of stratified flows ranging from three-dimensional turbulence to planetary scale circulations. Here we develop a framework for considering the multi-scale evolution of the local APE using a spatial filtering, or coarse-graining, approach. A scale decomposition valid generally for filters with both horizontal and vertical support is proposed, and shown to admit a construction in terms of a series of band-passed energies. The physical interpretation of the decomposition is discussed, and evolution equations for the APE at scales larger, and smaller, than the filtering scale are derived --- including the cross-scale APE flux term. These results can be paired with existing frameworks for coarse-grained kinetic energy, offering the potential for examining a complete energy cycle that accounts for conversions between both spatial scales and energy reservoirs. An illustrative example of the application of this approach to a simulation of three-dimensional Kelvin-Helmholtz instability is provided, including an exact formulation of the scale-dependent instability energy budgets, and the distribution of terms such as cross-scale transfers and APE dissipation in physical space.

papers.title: MAG-Net: Radar-Satellite Fusion for Severe Convective Nowcasting with Matched Evaluation of Satellite Contributions
papers.abstract: Radar-based nowcasting remains challenging for intense convective echoes because extrapolation cannot represent storm growth and decay, while regression-trained deep networks tend to smooth small-scale high-reflectivity structures. We present MAG-Net, a radar-satellite nowcasting framework that combines composite radar reflectivity with three Fengyun-4A (FY-4A) Advanced Geostationary Radiation Imager (AGRI) infrared fields through separate encoders and a Dual-Head decoder with Gradient-Preserving Fusion (GPF). We evaluate 73,928 spatial forecast windows, each covering a 90-minute forecast, from hourly initialization times across 122 severe-convective outbreaks over southeastern China in 2023. Matched variants separate the effects of output design and satellite input. For radar-only input, the critical success index (CSI) at 40 dBZ increases from 0.092 with regression output to 0.252 with Dual-Head/GPF. Adding AGRI fields under the same output design raises CSI at 40 dBZ to 0.273. The paired gain is 0.021, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.018-0.024 based on outbreak-level resampling. Object-based lifecycle evaluation shows satellite gains across growth, mature, and decay stages. At the 90-minute lead, the largest relative gain occurs before the birth of a new radar core, when radar-only skill is lowest. These findings show that the output formulation and the satellite observations contribute jointly, with the larger share of the severe-echo improvement coming from the output formulation, and identify when the satellite contribution is most pronounced.

papers.title: The role of the oceans for subseasonal prediction: insights from eddy-permitting and eddy-rich coupled forecast systems
papers.abstract: The oceans play a fundamental role in Earth's climate system, redistributing heat and influencing global and regional climate variability and predictability across weather and climate timescales. The benefits of ocean-atmosphere coupling for initialised predictions depend on the balance between improvements associated with more realistic air-sea interactions and dynamics, and degradations arising from the development of systematic biases at the coupling interface. Here, we draw on recent developments in modelling and data assimilation at ECMWF to revisit the role of ocean-atmosphere coupling in subseasonal predictions. In particular, we evaluate the impact of ocean-atmosphere coupling in 46-day reforecasts produced with the ECMWF Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) and explore the potential for improvements through increased horizontal resolution and a better representation of the ocean mesoscale. We find that ocean-atmosphere coupling significantly enhances ensemble forecast skill in the tropics, with positive effects increasing at longer lead times. In particular, Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) forecasts are substantially improved, with forecast skill extended by approximately 5 days compared to the uncoupled configuration. In contrast, ocean-atmosphere coupling has a more limited impact on the extratropical atmosphere at subseasonal timescales, with marginal impacts on the predictability of major tropospheric and stratospheric circulation indices. Finally, we present selected results from an experimental eddy-rich coupled configuration of the IFS, with a horizontal ocean resolution of approximately 8 km. We find that a better-resolved representation of the ocean mesoscale has a limited impact on atmospheric forecasts at subseasonal lead times, which suggests that many of the known deficiencies of the eddy-permitting reference configuration are mitigated by accurate initialisation.

papers.title: Quantifying AI data center nitrogen oxide (NO$_x$) emissions from space
papers.abstract: AI data center power demand is spurring rapid deployment of on- and near-site natural gas turbines. The resulting nitrogen oxide NO$_x$ pollution is a growing concern but has not previously been quantified with atmospheric observations. Here we demonstrate space-based detection and quantification of NO$_x$ emissions from the SpaceXAI Colossus 2 power plant in Southaven, Mississippi. Using observations from the geostationary TEMPO satellite instrument, we detect a strong increase in local mean NO$_2$ column concentrations after the plant began operations in late 2025. We then use TEMPO to estimate two-week-average NO$_x$ source rates from August 2025 to August 2026, calibrating against continuous emission monitoring system (CEMS) data from US power plants. TEMPO first detected NO$_x$ emissions in December 2025 at 530$\pm$220 kg h$^{-1}$. We find that emissions increased through August 2026, averaging 870$\pm$165 kg h$^{-1}$ after February 2026, roughly 19$\pm$4 times higher than expected from the facility's March 2026 permit for 41 turbines operating under best available control technology (BACT) requirements ($\sim$47 kg h$^{-1}$). Emissions at the expected level would be undetectable by our TEMPO analysis.
